messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 44
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Nurse
  trauma_type: Mugging or robbery
  pcl5: 68

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Mirror Checking: keep checking mirrors, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
  Memory: Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind., Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
  Negative Appraisals: No Good Ahead: Nothing good can happen to me anymore, Intrinsic Fault: There is something about me that made the event happen, Hopelessness: I have no future

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Arun is a 44-year-old married nurse who came to treatment months after being mugged on his way home from an evening hospital shift. The assault happened in the hospital parking structure, a place he had always treated as routine and forgettable. He remembers the fluorescent lights, the concrete pillar beside his car, and the sudden movement of a man coming out from between vehicles. What stays with him most are the visual fragments: a hand reaching, the flash of metal, the angle of the attacker’s face, the ground rushing up when he was struck. Even now he describes the event as if he is looking at photographs rather than remembering a continuous story, and when those images come back, he feels pain in the same places that were hurt during the robbery. The parking garage at work remains especially potent because it so closely matches the scene of the attack; finishing a shift and walking toward his car can make him feel as if he is stepping back into that same moment.

In the weeks after the mugging, Arun began to make sense of what happened in harsh, personal terms. He had come to believe there was something about him that made the event happen, as if he had looked weak, inattentive, or like an easy target. From there his view of the future narrowed quickly. He found himself thinking that nothing good could happen to him anymore and, more bleakly, that he had no future in any meaningful sense. Those conclusions did not stay abstract. Because he was certain the world had become permanently unsafe and that he himself was somehow marked for harm, he started living defensively: checking mirrors repeatedly, keeping his mind occupied whenever possible so he would not have to dwell on what had happened, and constantly scanning his surroundings for signs of threat.

That sense of danger spread into nearly every part of daily life. Arun began choosing seats in staff meetings, the break room, and restaurants based on whether his back was protected and whether he could see exits. Walking through the hospital corridors or crossing the parking lot, he looked behind him again and again to check whether someone was following. Nights became difficult; he struggled to fall asleep and woke easily, alert to minor sounds in the house. The more he felt under threat, the more convinced he became that his life had been permanently damaged. During long wakeful hours he would think that a man who could not even get to his car safely had no real future, and this fear-driven vigilance only tightened his need to monitor every space he entered.

His memory of the robbery did not soften with time. Instead, the continued sense of threat seemed to sharpen it. If he heard footsteps behind him after a shift or noticed his reflection unexpectedly in a glass door, vivid images of the assault would flare up with startling clarity. He would not simply remember being hit; he would feel the pain return in his body as though the attack were happening again. Those moments left him feeling sure that the mugging had changed him fundamentally. The fact that the images arrived so forcefully seemed, to Arun, like proof that he was broken beyond repair and that whatever future he had imagined for himself had already been cut off.

To manage this, he tried harder and harder to stay in control. He kept his mind busy constantly—podcasts during his commute, television left on at home, charting longer than necessary at work—anything to avoid an unoccupied moment. He checked mirrors repeatedly, including reflective surfaces in the unit, to reassure himself no one was approaching unnoticed. He scanned parking areas, hallways, and elevators for danger. Yet these habits seemed to keep the robbery close. Catching his own reflection while checking behind him could suddenly call up a frozen visual image of the attacker; relentless scanning made every movement in the periphery feel significant enough to pull the memory forward. Afterward he would judge himself even more severely, seeing his inability to put the event away as further evidence that there was something fundamentally wrong with him.

The cycle has begun to alter his work and home life in concrete ways. At the hospital he lingers until other staff are leaving so he does not have to walk alone, and when no protected seat is available he becomes distracted, tracking doors and footsteps more than conversations. His wife has noticed that even when they go out to eat, he studies mirrors and keeps choosing seats against the wall, rarely relaxing. Arun sought help only after realizing that his world had become organized around preventing another attack and around escaping the images of the first one, neither of which was working. What frightens him most is the thought that he is already living the rest of his life in that parking garage, with no future beyond vigilance; what he hopes, though he says it cautiously, is that he might somehow stop feeling hunted by both the world and his own mind.
